title: Norton's theorem and source transformation: the current-source twin of Thevenin
examples: How do I find a Norton equivalent?

parts.label: Short-circuit A
parts.ask: How do I find the Norton current?

explain.say: Thevenin gave us a battery plus a resistor. In 1926 Edward Norton at Bell Labs described the twin: a current source with a resistor beside it. A current source is a supply that pushes a fixed current whatever the load. We'll use the same network as before, with the load terminals joined by an ammeter.

parts.label: Short-circuit A
parts.ask: How do I find the Norton current?

explain.say: Step one: short the load terminals and measure the current. That is the Norton current. Now R3 sits in parallel with R2: 2 and 6 ohms make 1.5 ohms, plus R1 gives 4.5 ohms. The source pushes about 2.67 amps, which puts 4 volts across the pair, so R3 carries 4 over 2, which is 2 amps. Which resistor's current were we after?

parts.label: Short-circuit A
parts.ask: How do I find the Norton current?

explain.say: R3's, the short-circuit current. Step two: the Norton resistance is found exactly like the Thevenin one, sources off and looking back in, so it is the same 4 ohms. There's a lovely shortcut too: the open-circuit voltage divided by the short-circuit current. 8 volts over 2 amps gives 4 ohms. Do Thevenin and Norton always share the same resistance?

parts.label: Short-circuit A
parts.ask: How do I find the Norton current?

draw.text: R_N = R_th = V_oc / I_sc = 8 V / 2 A = 4 Ω

explain.say: Yes, always. Here are the twins side by side. Thevenin: 8 volts in series with 4 ohms. Norton: 2 amps in parallel with 4 ohms. Open the terminals and the Norton source's 2 amps all flows through the 4 ohms, making 8 volts. Short them and 2 amps comes out. Same in every test. Which form looks handier for loads in parallel?

draw.text: V_th = I_N × R_N = 2 A × 4 Ω = 8 V

explain.say: The Norton form, since its resistor is already in parallel. Swapping between them is called source transformation: a voltage source V with series R becomes a current source V over R with the same R in parallel, and back again. Well done! Exam tip: a chain of source transformations can shrink a ladder network without writing a single equation.

draw.text: V in series with R  ⇄  V/R in parallel with R

faq.a: Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by a current source I N in parallel with a resistance R N. I N is the short-circuit current and R N equals the Thevenin resistance.

faq.q: How do I find the Norton current?
faq.a: Short the output terminals with a wire and work out the current through that short. Here it is 2 amps.

faq.q: Is the Norton resistance the same as the Thevenin resistance?
faq.a: Yes. Both are found by switching off the sources and looking back in, and both equal the open-circuit voltage divided by the short-circuit current.
Replacing a voltage source V in series with R by a current source V over R in parallel with the same R, or the reverse. The two look identical from outside.

faq.a: An ideal current source pushes a fixed current whatever voltage that needs. A transistor in its active region behaves close to one.

quiz.say: A circuit has an open-circuit voltage of 15 volts and a short-circuit current of 3 amps. What is its Norton resistance?
quiz.show: A circuit has V_oc = 15 V and I_sc = 3 A. What is its Norton resistance?
quiz.why: R N is V oc over I sc: 15 over 3 gives 5 ohms.

wrong.2: That divides the current by the voltage, upside down.

quiz.say: Convert a 20 volt source in series with 4 ohms into a Norton source.
quiz.show: Convert 20 V in series with 4 Ω into a Norton source.
quiz.why: The current is V over R, 20 over 4, which is 5 amps, and the same 4 ohms goes in parallel.

wrong.1: That multiplies V by R instead of dividing.
wrong.2: The resistance stays 4 ohms; it does not become the voltage number.
